h1: The 6 Best Heavy-Duty Electric Pruning Shears of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Electric Pruning Shears: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six heavy-duty cordless electric pruning shears, from 1.65 to 2.75 inch cutting diameters, with battery and motor details.
summary: The ANTTCTIG 2.75 inch kit is the best heavy-duty electric pruning shear, with the widest cut here, two batteries and spare blades under $100. The 2.56 inch ANTTCTIG is nearly as capable. The SEESII adds four modes and a brushless motor, the SK7 blade model names its steel, and a budget brushless set and the KOMOK round out the list.
intro: Electric pruning shears sell on one number, the cutting diameter, and buyers routinely pay for capacity they never touch. A 2.75 inch bite matters on old orchard limbs, but for shrubs, roses and young fruit trees a smaller head is lighter in the hand and quicker at the bench. The rated diameter is also a ceiling, not a working size: cutting at the limit hour after hour strains the motor.

Six cordless models were ranked here on paper by cutting diameter, motor type, battery setup, blade details and control modes. Diameters and battery figures come from the listings, and prices are given as buckets. Where a listing leaves out the motor or battery type, we say so, because a spec that is missing is a decision you cannot make before checkout.

products.name: ANTTCTIG Electric Pruning Shears, 2.75'' Cut, 2 Batteries & Spare Blades
products.verdict: The largest cutting capacity in this group, with a full kit.
products.description:
The 2.75 inch ANTTCTIG is the biggest cutter in the group, and it comes as a full kit. It cuts branches up to 2.75 inches and ships with two batteries and spare blades, in the $50 to $100 bucket. Two batteries let you swap one while the other charges, and spare blades matter because a dull edge is the first thing to ruin a cutting day.

It wins because capacity is the widest here and the spare blades keep it running. The 2.56 inch sibling is almost as capable but a bit smaller.

Choose it for thick orchard limbs and old fruit trees. The caveats: a bigger head means more weight in the hand, and the listing does not name the motor type. Expect fatigue over a long day.

products.name: ANTTCTIG Electric Pruning Shears, 2.56'' Cut, 2 Batteries & Spare Blades
products.verdict: Nearly the same kit with a slightly smaller cut.
products.description:
The 2.56 inch ANTTCTIG is the same kit with a slightly smaller bite. It cuts up to 2.56 inches and includes two batteries and spare blades, in the $50 to $100 bucket. A difference of about 0.2 inches rarely decides a job, since most branches fall well below both ratings.

It follows the 2.75 inch model because the difference is small enough that most gardeners will not notice it. It gives up that margin for a slightly smaller head.

Best for general heavy pruning of trees and large shrubs. The caveat: the motor type is not listed, same as the larger model. If you routinely hit the thickest limbs, step up to the 2.75 inch; otherwise this is the sensible one.
products.skipIf: You need the very largest cut.

products.name: SEESII Electric Pruning Shears 4 Modes, 2.2" Cut Electric Pruners Cordless
products.verdict: Four modes for matching cut speed to branch thickness.
products.description:
The SEESII brings control. It has a 2.2 inch cutting diameter, a brushless motor and four modes, in the $100 to $200 bucket. Modes let you match cut speed to branch thickness: a quick snip for thin stems, a slower and stronger setting for thicker wood.

It takes third because it costs more than the ANTTCTIG pair, and the listing does not mention batteries. It handles thicker wood than smaller siblings, but its capacity is below the top two.

It suits mixed pruning of shrubs and fruit trees where branch sizes vary. The caveat is information: check the product page for the battery setup before ordering. Choose it for the brushless motor and the modes, not for capacity.

products.name: 2.1"/54mm Electric Pruning Shears, Upgraded Cordless Electric Scissors, Brushless Motor, Dual 2.0Ah Battery, Sk7 Blade, LCD Display for Heavy-Duty Garden, Orchard & Branch Cutter
products.verdict: The only one here that names its blade steel.
products.description:
This 2.1 inch (54mm) set is the one that names its steel. It has a brushless motor, an SK7 blade, an LCD display and dual 2.0Ah batteries, in the $50 to $100 bucket. SK7 is a carbon tool steel often used for blades, and naming it tells you something about edge hardness that an unnamed blade does not.

It holds fourth because 2.1 inches is smaller than the ANTTCTIG models and the brand is unlisted. The LCD adds a battery readout.

It suits orchard owners who like to see battery level at a glance. Expect a smaller cut than the top two. The caveat: with no brand named, check the warranty and returns before ordering, and confirm that spare blades are sold.

products.name: Electric Pruning Shears, Upgraded 2.1" Cutting Garden Shears with LCD Display, Brushless Motor
products.verdict: A 2.1 inch brushless kit with an LCD and two batteries.
products.description:
The budget brushless set matches the SK7 model on spec but not on detail. It offers a 2.1 inch cutting diameter, a brushless motor, an LCD display and two 2Ah batteries, in the $50 to $100 bucket. Brushless motors have no carbon brushes to wear out, so they tend to run cooler and last longer.

It lands fifth because it matches the specs of the SK7 model above but does not name its blade steel. Generic branding adds some uncertainty.

Choose it for backyard fruit trees and hedges. Buy it only if the price is below the SK7 version. The caveat is that blade quality is unspecified, so you may replace the blade sooner than on a named steel, and brand support is thin.

products.name: KOMOK Electric Pruning Shears, Professional Cordless Electric Pruners Battery Powered Tree Branch Cutter, 1.65" (42mm) Cutting Diameter
products.verdict: Smaller cut, but a stated 8 to 10 hour runtime.
products.description:
The KOMOK is the long-day option. It has a 1.65 inch (42mm) cutting diameter, two 2Ah batteries and a listed 8 to 10 hour runtime, in the $100 to $200 bucket. A smaller head is lighter, which is the quiet advantage on a day spent holding a tool overhead.

It brings up the rear because its capacity is the smallest here and it costs more than the ANTTCTIG pair. The runtime claim is the draw, but treat it as the maker's number, not something we can verify.

Best for vineyard or orchard days with lighter wood. The caveat: it will not handle thick branches, and the price is the highest bracket here. If you prune anything over about 1.5 inches, take the ANTTCTIG instead.

whatMatters.detail: This is the thickest branch the blade can cut, as rated by the maker. Running at the limit strains the motor, so pick a model with at least half an inch spare over your usual branch size. Check the number in the title, and remember that dry hardwood cuts harder than green wood, so the practical limit is lower for dead branches.

Brushless motors have no carbon brushes to wear out, so they tend to run cooler and last longer. They usually cost more. The saving shows up over seasons of use. Look for the word brushless in the title, as on the SEESII and the two 2.1 inch sets, and treat unlisted motor types as unknown, since the ANTTCTIG pair does not state one.

A 2Ah battery stores less than a 4Ah one, so runtime is shorter. Two batteries let you swap mid-job, which matters on a long day. Check the Ah and count in the listing, and look at whether a charger is included, since some bundles omit it, and keep the charger where you can reach it.

Spare blades extend a kit's useful life, since a dull blade slows work and strains the motor. A named steel such as SK7 hints at hardness. Look for spares and the steel name in the listing, and check that replacement blades are sold separately, because a bundled spare runs out.

Modes let you change cut speed, and an LCD shows battery. Both are conveniences, not necessities, and neither changes the cut. Check which you actually want before paying more, because the plain ANTTCTIG kits skip both and still offer the widest cut and two batteries, and extras raise the price.

faq.q: Are electric pruners safe for beginners?
faq.a: Yes with care. Keep fingers clear of the blade and remove the battery when changing blades. Wear gloves, and do not hold branches with your free hand while cutting. Keep the safety lock on between cuts.

Cutting branches near the maximum diameter all day. That overheats the motor and wears the blade, so keep thicker cuts to a minimum on the ANTTCTIG models, and switch to a saw when the limb is near the rating.

Generally yes for frequent use because there are no brushes to wear. For occasional use it matters less, and the SEESII or the 2.1 inch sets add it at modest cost, while the ANTTCTIG pair does not state a motor type.

faq.q: How do I set up the battery?
faq.a: Charge fully before first use and lock the battery into the handle. Check the blade guard, test on a thin twig, and carry the second battery if you have one so a long day does not stall.

faq.q: How do I maintain the blades?
faq.a: Clean sap after use and apply a light oil to the blade. A dull or sticky blade slows the motor, so wipe it between jobs and store the shears with the blade closed.
They can cut up to their rated diameter, but dry hard wood is tougher. Stay below the limit, and use a saw for the thickest dead branches, which can stall the blade.

finalTake: Buy the 2.75 inch ANTTCTIG for thick orchard limbs, or the 2.56 inch if you do not need the last fraction of an inch. The SEESII suits mixed pruning with varied speeds, the SK7 and budget brushless sets suit backyard trees, and the KOMOK suits long days on thin wood. Run any of them below the stated limit.
